item.title: NATS-as-C2: Inside a new technique attackers are using to harvest cloud credentials and AI API keys
item.description:
Sysdig researchers identify first known case of NATS-as-C2: attackers exploit CVE-2026-33017 in Langflow to deploy cloud-native messaging infrastructure for distributed credential harvesting targeting AWS and AI API keys.
Technical details: • CVE-2026-33017 exploitation in Langflow enables initial compromise • NATS server used as C2 with pub/sub orchestration and durable task queues • Distributed worker pool architecture for scalable credential hunting operations • Primary targets: AWS access keys and AI service API credentials • Cloud-native messaging bypasses traditional C2 detection methods
Attack methodology: • Leverages legitimate NATS messaging protocol to blend with normal traffic • Pub/sub model enables real-time task distribution across compromised hosts • Durable queues ensure persistence of harvesting tasks during network interruptions • Workers coordinate autonomously through message broker infrastructure
DFIR opportunities: • Monitor for unusual NATS client connections and message broker traffic patterns • Hunt for Langflow instances with CVE-2026-33017 indicators • Analyze cloud authentication logs for bulk credential validation attempts
Detection focus: Identify NATS protocol traffic (port 4222) from unexpected sources and correlate with cloud service authentication anomalies.

item.title: Shai-Hulud Part 2: When the Worm Forged Its Own Security Certificate by Lucie Cardiet
item.description:
TeamPCP open-sourced Shai-Hulud supply-chain worm with enhanced OIDC token extraction capability. New variant forges legitimate Sigstore certificates during CI/CD compromise, bypassing SLSA Build Level 3 provenance checks across 170+ npm packages.
Key technical details: - Extracts ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN from GitHub Actions runner memory - Uses stolen OIDC token to obtain valid X.509 certificates from Sigstore's Fulcio CA - Produces legitimate cosign signatures and SLSA provenance attestations for malicious packages - Exfiltrates to git-tanstack[.]com lookalike domain and Session Network endpoints - 44 GitHub forks within hours, including FreeBSD port expanding target platforms
Attack methodology: - Infiltrates via dependency installation during CI/CD pipeline execution - Performs lateral movement through GitHub OIDC → Sigstore CA → npm registry trust chain - Each authentication event appears legitimate in individual audit logs - Bypasses artifact scanning due to valid attestations and functional package code
DFIR artifacts: - OIDC token requests + Sigstore Fulcio API calls in same runner session - Anomalous outbound connections during CI jobs with package publishing - Cross-correlation needed across GitHub Actions logs, network traces, and npm publish events
Hunt for CI runners making unexpected Sigstore API calls combined with unfamiliar network destinations in the same job execution timeline.

item.title: Another Crack in the Chain of Trust: Uncovering (Yet Another) Secure Boot Bypass
item.description:
Binarly Research exposes CVE-2025-3052 (BRLY-2025-001): memory corruption in Microsoft-signed UEFI module enables arbitrary memory writes and complete Secure Boot bypass on most UEFI systems.
Critical technical details: • Affects 14 modules signed with "Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011" certificate - same cert used for Linux shim bootloader • Root cause: unsafe handling of IhisiParamBuffer NVRAM variable allows arbitrary memory write primitive • Attack overwrites gSecurity2 global variable to disable Secure Boot enforcement during boot process • Originally DT Research BIOS flashing tool (Dtbios-efi64-71.22.efi), signed October 2022, discovered on VirusTotal November 2024 • Insyde-based devices protected due to variable locking, but all other UEFI systems vulnerable
Attack methodology: • Privileged attacker sets malicious IhisiParamBuffer value from OS • Registers vulnerable module + unsigned payload module in UEFI Boot Manager • On reboot, vulnerable module executes during BDS phase, overwrites security checks • Unsigned payload executes with Secure Boot appearing enabled to OS
Impact enables bootkit installation before OS loads, bypassing all OS-level defenses. Microsoft added 14 hashes to Secure Boot dbx on June 10, 2025 Patch Tuesday.
Update Secure Boot dbx immediately. Hunt for unexpected UEFI modules in Boot Manager and monitor NVRAM variable modifications.

item.title: CVE-2026-44843: One Chat Message Steals Your Credentials. Then It Gets Worse!
item.description:
CVE-2026-44843: Single chat message triggers unauthenticated credential exfiltration from LangChain applications via malicious object deserialization in tracer component. CVSS not specified, but enables full workspace takeover.
Key technical details: • Exploits broad object deserialization in langchain-core tracer paths (_exit_history, astream_log, astream_events v1) using load(run.inputs, allowed_objects="all") • Attack payload: JSON dict with HubRunnable constructor that omits api_key, forcing fallback to LANGSMITH_API_KEY environment variable • Vulnerable paths: RunnableWithMessageHistory, astream_log(), astream_events(version="v1") in public LangServe endpoints • 94 registered serializable classes were potential gadgets for constructor-based side effects
Attack methodology: • Attacker sends structured chat message mimicking LangChain serialized object format • Framework preserves dict structure in run.inputs without sanitization • Tracer calls load() during object revival, instantiating HubRunnable • Constructor triggers LangSmith client creation with attacker-controlled api_url • Client reads production API key from environment, sends in x-api-key header to attacker URL
DFIR artifacts: • Outbound HTTP requests to suspicious domains with x-api-key headers containing "lsv2_pt_" tokens • Process execution of langsmith-py client with network connections during chat processing

item.title: How to Detect Persistence Mechanisms with Elastic SIEM: SOC Analyst Hands-On Lab | Hunt Forward Lab…
item.description:
New hands-on DFIR lab teaches persistence mechanism hunting in Elastic SIEM using realistic CartFlow Commerce breach scenario. Three-week attacker dwell time with registry run keys, scheduled tasks, and startup folder redundancy detected through ES|QL correlation.
Detailed breakdown: • Covers MITRE T1547.001 (Registry Run Keys), T1053.005 (Scheduled Tasks), T1060 (Startup Folder) persistence techniques • Lab uses 30-day persistence-lab-logs dataset with buried attacker activity across developer workstations • Attack timeline: Registry run key April 7th 2AM → scheduled task April 11th → startup folder April 18th • ES|QL queries detect off-hours registry writes to HKCU\Run pointing to AppData binaries, shell-spawned schtasks.exe with SYSTEM privileges, executable drops to Windows Startup folders
Hunt patterns include: • Time-based analysis: `DATE_EXTRACT("HOUR_OF_DAY", @timestamp)` flags 2AM-5AM activity • Path risk scoring: AppData/ProgramData binary locations vs legitimate Program Files • Process ancestry: cmd.exe/powershell.exe spawning schtasks.exe indicates manual attacker activity • Campaign scope correlation: `COUNT_DISTINCT(mechanism)` across hosts reveals redundant persistence deployment
Complete with Sigma detection rule conversion and GitHub portfolio integration. Hunt notebook templates track IOCs, execution timelines, and affected host risk scoring for incident response prioritization.

item.title: Proxying the Unproxyable? Sending EXE traffic to a Proxy, (Wed, May 13th)
item.description:

Technical implementation: • Proxifier creates rules to route traffic by executable name (e.g., "send abc.exe to proxy A") • Supports direct connection or SOCKS5 proxy redirection with configurable logging • Bypasses TLS 1.3 encryption limitations where packet captures only show encrypted data • Tool enables real-time monitoring of API calls and data transfers from target executables
Use cases for DFIR: • Analyze malware C2 communications hidden behind TLS encryption • Inspect suspicious executable network behavior without breaking encryption • Monitor API calls and data exfiltration attempts in controlled environments • Capture full HTTP/HTTPS request/response cycles for forensic documentation
Deploy in sandbox environments to analyze unknown executables. Route target process traffic through Burp Suite or similar proxy to capture plaintext API calls and reconstruct attack methodologies.

item.title: Undermining the trust boundary: Investigating a stealthy intrusion through third-party compromise
item.description:
Microsoft IR exposes sophisticated campaign exploiting third-party IT provider to deploy credential harvesting DLLs through legitimate HPE Operations Agent. Attackers maintained 123-day persistence using trusted systems, avoiding malware entirely.
Key technical details: • Malicious network provider "mslogon.dll" registered on DCs to intercept cleartext credentials via NPLogonNotify/NPPasswordChangeNotify APIs (T1199, T1556.002) • Password filter "passms.dll" deployed in LSA notification packages, exfiltrating Base64+custom encoded creds to C:\ProgramData\WindowsUpdateService\UpdateDir\Ipd • Web shells Errors.aspx and modified Signoff.aspx provided persistence on internet-facing servers WEB-01/WEB-02 • Ngrok tunnels established for covert RDP lateral movement, masking true C2 infrastructure • VBScript abc003.vbs deployed via HPE OA for AD/network discovery without triggering alerts
Attack leveraged compromised third-party service provider managing HPE Operations Manager, executing malicious scripts through legitimate automation channels. Campaign spanned 123 days with credential interception on multiple domain controllers.
Hunt for unsigned DLLs in LSA notification packages and network provider registry keys. Monitor for unexpected modifications to legitimate web application files and ngrok processes on internal servers.

item.title: How Dirty Frag rose from the Copy Fail exploit
item.description:
CVE-2026-31431 (Dirty Frag/Copy Fail) Linux kernel privilege escalation vulnerability was actively exploited 9+ days before public disclosure. ReversingLabs identified 163 unique samples across ELF binaries, Python scripts, and malicious PyPI packages.
Key technical details: • CVE-2026-31431 exploits kernel page-cache manipulation similar to Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847) for local privilege escalation • Earliest malicious sample observed April 29, 2026 - major surge began May 1 with 50+ samples overnight • Shellcode pattern uses compact syscalls: setuid(0), setgid(0), setgroups(0), then execve("/bin/sh") with TERM=xterm • Linux.Trojan.Multiverze family actively adopted the exploit; malicious PyPI wheel "copyfail" distributed via supply chain
Attack methodology (MITRE ATT&CK): • T1068: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation via kernel vulnerability • T1548.001: Abuse setuid/setgid mechanisms for root credential normalization • T1195.002: Supply chain compromise through malicious PyPI package distribution • T1059.004/.006: Unix shell and Python interpreter abuse for payload execution
DFIR artifacts and detection: • V4bel reference implementation uses distinctive opcode patterns: b06a0f05 (setgid), b0690f05 (setuid), b0740f05 (setgroups) • Co-occurrence of /bin/sh and TERM=xterm strings with syscall patterns provides high-confidence detection • AV detection rates currently 2-17 scanners, indicating signature gap

item.title: State-sponsored actors, better known as the friends you don’t want
item.description:
State-sponsored actors exploit trust boundaries using legitimate tools and credentials, requiring fundamentally different IR approaches than ransomware response. They operate for months undetected, using PowerShell, WMI, and existing admin tools rather than custom malware.
Key operational differences: • Reconnaissance phase lasts weeks/months using OSINT and social engineering, often leaving zero artifacts in defender logs • Initial access via legitimate credentials from spear phishing or supply chain compromise - no exploit signatures • Lateral movement through trusted tools (SCCM, Puppet, PowerShell AD queries) that appear as routine admin tasks • Multiple persistence mechanisms across infrastructure: scheduled tasks, service configs, dormant accounts, firmware implants • Anti-forensics includes log clearing, timestamp manipulation, memory-only operations, and false flag attribution
Critical preparedness gaps: • Default logging insufficient - enable Windows process creation (4688), PowerShell script block logging (4104), deploy Sysmon on critical systems • Behavioral baselines must be continuously updated to reflect organizational changes and seasonal patterns • Out-of-band communications essential - assume adversary can monitor internal IR channels if they have domain admin • OT/ICS environments need hardware-enforced unidirectional gateways, not software-defined segmentation

item.title: How to respond to an incident in Kubernetes | EKS | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
EKS containers are ephemeral - when pods crash, logs vanish forever unless shipped to CloudWatch beforehand. New guide details forensic artifacts and containment strategies for Kubernetes breaches.
Key technical details: • EKS logging sources: API server logs, audit logs, authenticator logs (RBAC/IAM), controller manager, scheduler, and application logs • Non-EKS sources: CloudTrail (lateral movement detection), VPC Flow logs (C2 traffic), GuardDuty alerts • Critical artifacts: /var/log/pods directory on worker nodes, memory dumps from compromised containers • Detection queries for kubectl exec abuse: filter requestURI containing "/exec" in kube-apiserver-audit logs
Containment strategy: • Apply "Deny-All" NetworkPolicy to quarantine infected pods while preserving forensic evidence • Remove pod labels to stop load balancer traffic routing • Rotate compromised authentication credentials immediately • Replace infected containers entirely - treat as cattle, not pets
Real-world case: TraderTraitor (North Korean 🇰🇵 APT) pivoted from phished EKS cluster to cryptocurrency exchange financial systems via exposed service account tokens.
Enable comprehensive EKS logging before incidents occur. Query CloudWatch for suspicious kubectl exec and secrets access patterns.
